case_study_insert.main_stem: Pine Ridge Textiles (PRT) is a private limited company in the textile manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Elowen Penrose, the firm weaves recycled-fibre fabrics for clothing brands and runs a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. PRT plans to invest $720,000 in an automated weaving loom, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 from a new share issue. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.20 a unit and a selling price of $9.70, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. PRT faces a rising defect rate of 2.4% on the new loom and skilled-operator absenteeism, which threatens its delivery schedules to clothing brands.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The weaving line produced 18,400 metres of cloth last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 4.0% a year earlier. Customer returns fell from 52 to 28 per month and average order lead time is 5.6 days. A survey of 450 clothing buyers found that 61% prefer fabrics made with recycled fibre and 48% will pay up to $0.50 more. A skills audit shows 16 of 60 operators have not received on-the-job training on the new looms; external machine-training courses cost $750 per worker.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Pine Ridge Textiles as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, lifting borrowing costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 5.8% from $12.80 to $13.54 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale cotton and dye input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while clothing retail spending grew 2.9%.

questions.question_text: PRT plans to fund its $720,000 loom with a $420,000 bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for PRT of raising the $300,000 through a share issue rather than a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings in $300,000 of permanent equity that carries no interest charge and no fixed repayment dates. Unlike the $420,000 bank loan, it does not add to PRT's interest burden, so the rise in the base rate from 4.25% to 5.00% cannot increase the cost of this part of the $720,000 loom. With fixed costs of $216,000 a year already to cover, avoiding extra interest protects the $4.50 contribution earned on each of the 80,000 units and leaves more cash to tackle the 2.4% defect rate.

Point 2: Equity does not have to be secured against PRT's assets, so the weaving business is not exposed to repossession if the new loom takes time to bed in. A larger bank loan would require collateral and covenants that could constrain Elowen Penrose's decisions as the firm expands. The new shareholders also supply $300,000 that can be spent on the loom immediately, speeding the shift to recycled-fibre fabrics that 61% of the 450 surveyed buyers prefer, which supports the $9.70 selling price and helps win more clothing-brand orders.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of equity finance identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PRT, its $720,000 loom and its costs.

questions.question_text: PRT wants to promote its recycled-fibre fabrics to clothing brands. Consider sponsoring a fashion trade fair, a social media campaign with eco-influencers, or direct mail to clothing brands. Which should PRT choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Fashion trade fair sponsorship: A trade fair puts PRT's recycled-fibre fabrics directly in front of clothing-brand buyers and design teams, allowing the 18,400 metres of cloth to be inspected, which matters when the defect rate is 2.4% and buyers worry about consistency. It also lets Elowen Penrose negotiate on the spot. The drawbacks are high stand and travel costs for a firm already funding a $720,000 loom, and only a small, geographically limited audience attends.

Social media eco-influencer campaign: This reaches the 61% of 450 surveyed buyers who prefer recycled fibre and the 48% who would pay $0.50 more, at low cost per contact and with measurable engagement. Influencers can tell the sustainability story behind the new loom and build consumer pull that pushes clothing brands to stock PRT. The limits are slower conversion into bulk orders and reliance on influencer credibility; a viral post does not guarantee the steady 80,000-unit volume the loom is meant to deliver.

Direct mail to clothing brands: Targeted letters and fabric samples reach decision-makers cheaply and can be followed up personally, which suits a private limited company selling to a small number of known accounts. Response rates are usually low, however, and mail cannot build the consumer awareness that makes brands request PRT by name; it also misses the 48% premium segment entirely.

Recommendation: PRT should choose the social media eco-influencer campaign. It directly matches the 61% and 48% research findings and the $0.50 premium, costs far less than a trade fair, and creates consumer pull that a narrow direct-mail list cannot. The trade fair is rejected as expensive and too small for a 60-employee firm funding a $720,000 loom; direct mail is rejected as low-response and unable to build the awareness needed to sell 80,000 units. PRT can add one trade fair later once demand is proven.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to PRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of PRT with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discussion of all three options in context with a justified recommendation explaining why the trade fair and direct mail are rejected.

questions.question_text: PRT uses autocratic leadership in a hierarchical structure and still faces skilled-operator absenteeism and a 2.4% defect rate. Explain two benefits for PRT of introducing democratic leadership on the weaving floor.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 operators a voice in how the new automated loom is run, so those who handle the recycled-fibre fabrics daily can suggest settings that reduce the 2.4% defect rate. Involvement raises job satisfaction and commitment, which should cut the skilled-operator absenteeism that currently disrupts the 80,000-unit output plan and deliveries to clothing brands.

Point 2: Consulting operators also helps the 16 staff who still need on-the-job training on the looms. When workers help shape the training and routines, they accept the $750 external courses more readily and share knowledge with colleagues, lifting skills across the workforce of 60. Higher morale makes trained staff less likely to leave, protecting the $720,000 loom investment and the $4.50 contribution on every unit produced.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to PRT's defect rate, absenteeism and output.

questions.question_text: Sixteen of PRT's 60 operators still need training on the new loom. Consider on-the-job training on the loom or external machine-training courses costing $750 per worker. Which should PRT choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning beside the new loom is specific to PRT's own recycled-fibre fabrics and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps the 16 trainees producing while they learn, protecting output of 80,000 units and helping bring the 2.4% defect rate down. Trainers are experienced operators, so advice is immediate. However, good and bad habits pass on together, certification is limited, and the trainers' own work suffers, a real cost when absenteeism is already a problem.

External courses at $750 per worker: A structured course gives all 16 operators recognised certification and up-to-date machine knowledge, costing 16 × $750 = $12,000, affordable against the $720,000 loom. It removes staff from the floor temporarily, reducing capacity and perhaps delaying orders, and generic content may not match PRT's exact loom settings, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: PRT should choose on-the-job training first, backed by short external courses for the senior operators who will train the others. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output from a workforce of 60 already stretched by absenteeism; the full $12,000 external route is rejected because it cuts capacity exactly when the loom must deliver 80,000 units, and certification alone does not guarantee fewer defects. As the line stabilises, PRT can send remaining staff on the $750 courses.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to PRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in PRT's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how the management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $216,000 ÷ ($9.70 − $5.20) = $216,000 ÷ $4.50 = 48,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 48,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.70 − $5.20 = $4.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PRT's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 48,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 80,000 units: the margin of safety is 32,000 units, so the loom is comfortably profitable and PRT can decide whether to run it at full capacity.
2. Use the $4.50 contribution to model pricing. The research shows buyers would pay $0.50 more, so a rise from $9.70 to $10.20 lifts contribution to $5.00 a unit; managers can weigh this against the $216,000 fixed costs.
3. Use unit cost of $7.90 ($216,000 ÷ 80,000 = $2.70, plus $5.20 variable cost) to benchmark each quarter and target the 2.4% defect rate that creates rework waste.
4. Use labour productivity of about 1,333 units per worker (80,000 ÷ 60) to judge whether operator absenteeism is affordable and whether the $720,000 loom needs more staff.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 48,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 32,000-unit margin of safety; pricing from the $0.50 premium and $216,000 fixed costs; unit cost $7.90 to attack the 2.4% defect rate; labour productivity of about 1,333 units per worker for staffing.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PRT's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has PRT's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.65 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.85 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $90,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $300,000; 2025 current assets = $160,000 + $120,000 + $50,000 = $330,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $300,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.50; the 2025 comparison is $330,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.65. The stock-excluding measure for 2024 is ($300,000 − $150,000) ÷ $200,000 = $150,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.75; for 2025 it is ($330,000 − $160,000) ÷ $200,000 = $170,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.85.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. Current assets rose from $300,000 to $330,000 while current liabilities stayed at $200,000, so the 2024 figure of 1.50 and 2025 figure of 1.65 show a wider cushion of short-term assets. More importantly, the stock-excluding measure improved from 0.75 to 0.85, so PRT is less dependent on selling inventories of $150,000 to $160,000 to pay what it owes. That matters while it services a $420,000 bank loan and has committed $720,000 to the new loom. The warning sign is cash: it fell from $60,000 to $50,000 even as trade receivables climbed from $90,000 to $120,000, tying up more of the firm's short-term wealth in unpaid invoices from clothing brands. If those customers pay late, the stronger headline liquidity could reverse quickly, and the 2.4% defect rate could add rework costs just when the loom is bedding in.

Conclusion: PRT's financial position has improved. Both the 2024 and 2025 measures (1.50 to 1.65 and 0.75 to 0.85) point to stronger short-term solvency, and the gain is not driven only by inventory. The residual risk is slower collection of the $120,000 of trade receivables, so PRT should tighten credit control before the $720,000 loom investment puts further pressure on cash.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on whether financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PRT of switching its fabrics to recycled fibre.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The research supports a premium: 61% of the 450 buyers prefer recycled fibre and 48% would pay $0.50 more, so PRT can lift its $9.70 selling price and protect the $4.50 contribution per unit even as cotton and dye input costs rise 9.6%. It also differentiates PRT when dealing with clothing brands, helping secure the volume needed to justify the $720,000 loom.

Disadvantage: Recycled fibre may cost more or vary in quality, pushing the $5.20 variable cost per unit up and squeezing the $4.50 contribution. If the loom produces inconsistent recycled-fibre cloth, the 2.4% defect rate could rise, creating waste and rework just as PRT tries to deliver 80,000 units. Recycled-fibre suppliers may also be less reliable, threatening the 5.6-day lead time promised to clothing brands.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PRT's research, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in cotton and dye input costs will affect PRT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If PRT's $420,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 × $420,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $216,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may make clothing brands cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing, but PRT can reduce this risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.54 an hour): Much of the workforce of 60 is likely to be hourly-paid, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or each worker's pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 80,000 units ÷ 60 workers = about 1,333 units per worker. If the $720,000 loom lifts output per worker the higher wage is affordable; if absenteeism and the 2.4% defect rate hold productivity down, unit labour cost rises and the $4.50 contribution shrinks.

Cotton and dye input costs (9.6%): These feed the $5.20 variable cost per unit, but the insert never splits that cost, so only a labelled bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.6%, that is 9.6% × $5.20 = about $0.50 per unit; across 80,000 units that is roughly $40,000 a year (80,000 × $0.50). The 48% of buyers willing to pay $0.50 more and the 61% preferring recycled fibre give some pricing room, but clothing retail spending grew only 2.9%, so passing on the full rise may lose orders.

Conclusion: The 9.6% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 80,000 units and directly erodes the $4.50 contribution that justifies the $720,000 loom; the interest rise is at most a known $3,150, and the wage rise can be offset by the productivity gains the new loom is meant to deliver.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to PRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on PRT's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
